scenes.narration: The legacy of Petr Fiala outlived the circumstances that produced it. Fiala was first elected to the Chamber of Deputies as a non-partisan in the 2013 election. He won the 2014 Civic Democratic Party leadership election, promising to reform the party and regain public trust after a corruption scandal involving Prime Minister Petr Nečas.

Few lives travel as far as that of Petr Fiala, and the distance is the point. Fiala's party finished a distant second place in the 2017 parliamentary election, and remained in opposition despite multiple offers from the incoming Prime Minister Andrej Babiš to participate in his governing coalition. In 2020, Fiala led the initiative for a centre-right electoral alliance with KDU-ČSL and TOP 09, known as Spolu.

The childhood of Petr Fiala contains the adult in small print. He became its candidate for the premiership in the 2021 Czech parliamentary election, running on a pro-Western and pro-European centre-right platform, focused on fiscal responsibility and closer relations with NATO as part of Atlanticism. The alliance outperformed initial opinion polls and received the highest number of votes in the election, though with one seat fewer in the Chamber of Deputies than second-placed ANO 2011.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Petr Fiala — in that order. Under Fiala's leadership, Spolu formed a coalition agreement with the Pirates and Mayors alliance, with a majority of 108 of 200 seats. Fiala imposed sanctions on Russia and pushed to block Russian citizens from travelling to the European Union.

The turning point in the life of Petr Fiala looked like a failure at the time. In 2022, the Czech Republic held the presidency of the Council of the European Union. Fiala's administration also faced rising inflation and resulting decline of real wages, wider concerns about the economy and the ongoing global energy crisis.

Every biography of Petr Fiala has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. Throughout his term, Fiala's government has seen approval ratings in the low 20s. He led the Spolu alliance into the 2025 election in which his governing coalition lost its majority.

The education of Petr Fiala happened mostly outside any school. His paternal grandfather, František Fiala, was a lawyer who served as a senior councillor in the political administration of district governorates in Ostrava, Hodonín, and Olomouc during the First Czechoslovak Republic, and later as a state councillor in Brno. During World War II, a significant number of his relatives were deported to German concentration camps due to their Jewish heritage.

What Petr Fiala wanted at the start and what Petr Fiala got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Fiala has often cited his family's experience with both Nazi and Communist totalitarianism as a fundamental influence on his political views and his commitment to democracy. Fiala studied history and Czech language at the Faculty of Literature of Masaryk University between 1983 and 1988, and after graduating he worked as a historian in a local museum in Kroměříž.

The defining trait of Petr Fiala was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. In 1996, he became a docent at Charles University in Prague, and in 2002 he was named as the first professor of political science in the Czech Republic. In 2004, he became dean of the Faculty of Social Studies at Masaryk University, and in the same year was elected as rector of the university, defeating Jan Wechsler in the third round.

Those who met Petr Fiala at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. Fiala was reelected in 2008 and remained in the position until 2011. While Fiala was rector, Masaryk University increased its enrollment to around 45,000 students, became the most popular Czech university in terms of applications, and created a nationwide system for detecting academic plagiarism.

The private years of Petr Fiala explain the public decades better than any speech. During this period, Masaryk University built a new €220 million campus for biomedicine, opened a research station in Antarctica, and established the Central European Institute of Technology (CEITEC) using CZK 5.3 billion from the European Structural and Investment Funds. Between 1984 and 1989, he participated in the so-called underground university, hosting seminars in Brno focused on political philosophy.

The family Petr Fiala came from matters more than the legends admit. He was involved in unofficial Christian activities, especially in the circle of secretly consecrated Bishop Stanislav Krátký. Along with other Brno students, he founded the samizdat university magazine Revue 88, published in 1988–1989.

The first real success of Petr Fiala arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. After November 1989, Fiala continued his publishing and civic activism, working as an editor for magazines such as Proglas, Revue Politika, and Kontexty. In 1993, he founded the Centre for the Study of Democracy and Culture (CDK), a civic think-tank.

The last chapter of Petr Fiala was written long after the fame. Fiala was criticized for his activities during the 2021 election campaign because the centre was accepting state subsidies. Fiala has been active for a long time in institutions and bodies related to higher education and research in the Czech Republic and abroad.

The whole life of Petr Fiala reads like a single decision repeated. He served as vice-chair of the Czech Rectors' Conference from 2005 until 2009, and chair between 2009 and 2011. Fiala was a member of the council of the European University Association between 2009 and 2011.

Between the birth and the legend of Petr Fiala lie the years that actually decide it. In 2007, he was elected by the Chamber of Deputies to the council of the Institute for the Study of Totalitarian Regimes, where he served for five years. He is a member of many scientific and academic councils of public and private universities and research institutions in the Czech Republic and abroad.

The reputation of Petr Fiala was built in the middle, not at the edges. He has received a number of awards for his scientific and academic work; in 2011 he was awarded the Golden Plaque of the President of the Republic. In September 2011, Fiala served as chief aide for science to Prime Minister Petr Nečas, and was appointed as Minister of Education, Youth and Sports in Nečas' government on 2 May 2012, remaining in that post until Nečas resigned in 2013.

Somebody like Petr Fiala should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. In the 2013 parliamentary election, Fiala was elected as an independent to the Chamber of Deputies. The Civic Democratic Party (ODS) was defeated in the election and Fiala joined the party in November 2013.

The life of Petr Fiala begins far from where the story usually starts. In 2014, Fiala announced his candidacy for the leadership of ODS, and was elected as the party's fourth leader on 18 January. Fiala led ODS into the 2017 parliamentary election, in which the party finished second with 11% of the vote.

Petr Fiala was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. He refused to negotiate with ANO 2011 about joining the subsequent government, and ODS remained in opposition. On 28 November 2017, Fiala was elected Deputy President of the Chamber of Deputies, receiving 116 of 183 votes.

To understand where Petr Fiala ended up, start with where Petr Fiala began. With Fiala as leader, ODS made gains in the 2018 municipal elections and won the Senate election of the same year. Fiala then started negotiating with KDU-ČSL and TOP 09 about forming an electoral alliance for the parliamentary election in 2021.

The road from the beginning to the peak of Petr Fiala ran through years nobody filmed. ODS, KDU-ČSL and TOP 09 reached an agreement to form an alliance called Spolu ("Together"). Ahead of the election, opinion polls suggested that ANO 2011 would win, but in an electoral upset Spolu won the highest number of votes, and opposition parties won a majority of seats in the Chamber of Deputies.

Each stage of the life of Petr Fiala made the next stage possible. The opposition parties signed a memorandum agreeing to nominate Fiala for the position of prime minister. On 8 November, five Czech parties, ranging from the liberal-conservative Civic Democrats to the centre-left liberal Pirate Party, signed a pact to form a new centre-right coalition government and pledged to cut budget deficits.

The people who knew Petr Fiala young describe someone already restless. On 9 November, President Miloš Zeman formally asked Fiala to form a new government. On 17 November 2021, Fiala introduced Zeman to his proposed cabinet and Zeman agreed to appoint Fiala the new prime minister the same year on 26 November.

What Petr Fiala built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. In November 2021, Fiala confirmed that he would like to continue with the Spolu coalition into the 2022 Senate and municipal elections. On 28 November 2021, President Miloš Zeman appointed Petr Fiala as the 13th Prime Minister of the Czech Republic.

By the time Petr Fiala reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. Following his appointment, Fiala said he believed his government would bring change and improve the lives of people in the Czech Republic, but that the next year would be difficult for many citizens and the Czech Republic itself. Fiala's government won a confidence vote in the Chamber of Deputies of the Czech Republic on 13 January 2022 by 106–86.

The rise of Petr Fiala was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. Following the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Petr Fiala and his government took a tough stance on Russia, pushing for the toughest sanctions against Russia and supporting Ukraine's accession to the European Union. After the invasion, the Czech Republic immediately began supplying weapons and humanitarian aid to Ukraine.

Setbacks came early for Petr Fiala, and the response to them is the real story. On 15 March 2022, Fiala, together with Polish Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki and Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Janša, visited Kyiv to meet with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in a display of support for Ukraine. In July 2022, he officially accepted the Presidency of the Council of the European Union on behalf of the Czech Republic.

The legacy of Petr Fiala outlived the circumstances that produced it. He delivered a speech on the floor of the European Parliament, in which he called for the defense of European values, continuing support for Ukraine, and the inclusion of nuclear energy as a renewable resource (which was subsequently approved by a vote from MEPs). On 6 October 2022, Fiala chaired the 1st European Political Community Summit in Prague.

Few lives travel as far as that of Petr Fiala, and the distance is the point. Starting from 2023, the Czech Republic went into recession, and subsequently continued to underperform economically relative to other European Union member states, which were showing signs of recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic. The Czech Republic also experienced high debt growth and a decrease in real wages.

The childhood of Petr Fiala contains the adult in small print. In October 2023, Fiala condemned the October 7 attacks, and expressed his support for Israel's right to self-defence and actions during the subsequent Gaza war. He said that Israel was "the only functioning democracy in the Middle East and is the key to stability in the region." On 25 October 2023, Fiala visited Israel to express solidarity with the country.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of Petr Fiala — in that order. Fiala described the Czech Republic as "Israel's voice in Europe" and systematically opposed UN and European Union resolutions that criticized Israel's actions or sought sanctions against Israel. Czech arms exports to Israel doubled between 2022 and 2024 under the government of Petr Fiala.

The turning point in the life of Petr Fiala looked like a failure at the time. During 2023, Fiala and his government encountered deeply negative ratings from the Czech public. In December 2023, Fiala's approval rating dropped to 16% in some polls, one of the lowest approval ratings among world leaders, and the lowest for a Czech Prime Minister since Petr Nečas.
